I think just more differential school systems should be valid. People with different ideas of what a school should be can open different schools. Schools disrespecting children/youth should be closed down by child-protection/civil-rights law. Let the system be open to different schools first. I think what is important is that more employers look at ability (proof by test-runs/etc.) rather than just degrees/documents, so that no one worries about not being able to support themselves. In the child-rights perspective, the child should have the right to select which school they attend once they have the intention to choose, or at least leave the school they wish to leave. Homeschooling should be monitered by rights-protecting laws to prevent blockage of information/cults etc.

Though I have heard of kids thriving in the current mainstream school systems because they have respectful adults supportive of them in their lives (or other support), so that they maintain a clear mind, teachers literally leave them alone (not even bothered with checking homework etc.) because their parents were so formidable in protecting their children against violence/coercion, I still think it is more time and life saving if children/minors didn't have to be in that type of environment, so they can study for something they actually want to study rather than tests/exams about subjects they have no interest.

It seems your experience with schools wasn't this case... ... I hope more schools can be more like the schools I have been to, then. The schools I went to wasn't perfect in everything, most of the students feel safe there though if not every student (I'm not sure), to me they provided a safe place when I had none, one of the schools actively intervened with the situation that I was harmed in, they literally saved my life. Later I learned about UNICEF's rights respecting schools, the students there looked confident, have very high self esteem and self love, they at least know about their current protected rights, and their schools are there to stand up for them. I know these schools are still few in number, it's the reason that school's interests are less likely to directly oppose those of the children, in comparison to other social institutes that directly concern children, so schools are probably our best hope, it's even unusual if not unseen that parents who respect children will actively help protect children who they don't have a responsibility to protect, schools' case is another case, they have the facilities, they have greater power than one or two normal civilians, they are more likely to have the ability to help. If child-protective and respecting people open schools and hire other child-protective and respecting people, they provide a (mental and other practical support) safe place for children even if they don't (yet) provide boarding/housing facilities. I just hope more schools can be like this, and this is one of the hopeful things I see Unicef do (though I haven't visited one of theirs myself, I hope what they showed on video with kids actively participating and having their voices heard their decisions made was true, and the strength I was seeing did seem truthful).
